questions.answer: The transpose swaps rows and columns. The first row \((1,2)\) becomes the first column, and the second row \((3,4)\) becomes the second column. Therefore the transpose is \(\begin{pmatrix}1&3\\2&4\end{pmatrix}\).

The matrix is \(2\times 3\), so its transpose is \(3\times 2\). The columns of the transpose are the rows of the original matrix. Therefore the transpose is \(\begin{pmatrix}1&4\\2&5\\3&6\end{pmatrix}\).

questions.prompt: If A is \(4\times 7\), state the size of \(A^T\).
questions.answer: The transpose swaps the number of rows and columns. If A is \(4\times 7\), then \(A^T\) is \(7\times 4\).
The transpose rule is (\(A^T\))_ij = A_ji. Therefore (\(A^T\))_32 = A_23. In A, row 2 column 3 is 7. Therefore (\(A^T\))_32 = 7.

questions.prompt: Find the transpose of the column vector \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\-1\\4\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.answer: The transpose swaps rows and columns. A \(3\times 1\) column vector becomes a \(1\times 3\) row vector. Therefore the transpose is \(\begin{pmatrix}3&-1&4\end{pmatrix}\).

A matrix is symmetric when \(A^T\) = A. The off-diagonal entries must match. Here the top-right entry is 5 and the bottom-left entry is also 5. The diagonal entries stay fixed under transpose. Therefore \(A^T\) = A, so A is symmetric.

questions.prompt: Find all real x such that \(\begin{pmatrix}1&x\\3&4\end{pmatrix}\) is symmetric.
questions.answer: For a \(2\times 2\) matrix to be symmetric, the top-right entry must equal the bottom-left entry. Here those entries are x and 3. Therefore \(x=3\). With \(x=3\), the matrix equals its transpose.

First compute A + \(B=\begin{pmatrix}5&1\\5&5\end{pmatrix}\), so (A + B)^T = \(\begin{pmatrix}5&5\\1&5\end{pmatrix}\). Next compute \(A^T\) = \(\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\2&3\end{pmatrix}\) and \(B^T\) = \(\begin{pmatrix}4&5\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}\). Their sum is \(\begin{pmatrix}5&5\\1&5\end{pmatrix}\). Both sides are equal, so (A + B)^T = \(A^T\) + \(B^T\) for these matrices.

questions.prompt: For \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}\) and \(B=\begin{pmatrix}0&5\\6&7\end{pmatrix}\), compute (\(AB\))^T and \(B^T\) \(A^T\) to verify the transpose product rule.
questions.answer: First compute \(AB\) = \(\begin{pmatrix}1\cdot 0 + 2\cdot 6&1\cdot 5 + 2\cdot 7\\3\cdot 0 + 4\cdot 6&3\cdot 5 + 4\cdot 7\end{pmatrix}\) = \(\begin{pmatrix}12&19\\24&43\end{pmatrix}\). Therefore (\(AB\))^T = \(\begin{pmatrix}12&24\\19&43\end{pmatrix}\). Now \(B^T\) = \(\begin{pmatrix}0&6\\5&7\end{pmatrix}\) and \(A^T\) = \(\begin{pmatrix}1&3\\2&4\end{pmatrix}\). Multiply \(B^T\) \(A^T\): \(\begin{pmatrix}0\cdot 1 + 6\cdot 2&0\cdot 3 + 6\cdot 4\\5\cdot 1 + 7\cdot 2&5\cdot 3 + 7\cdot 4\end{pmatrix}\) = \(\begin{pmatrix}12&24\\19&43\end{pmatrix}\). The results match.

questions.prompt: A student claims (\(AB\))^T = \(A^T\) \(B^T\) for all square matrices. Use \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(B=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\) to diagnose the error.
questions.answer: Compute \(AB\) = \(\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\), so (\(AB\))^T = \(\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\). Now compute \(A^T\) = \(\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(B^T\) = \(\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\). Then \(A^T\) \(B^T\) = \(\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}\). This is not equal to (\(AB\))^T. The correct rule reverses the order: (\(AB\))^T = \(B^T\) \(A^T\).
